title: Bubble Sort
directAnswer: Nested loops: on each pass compare adjacent pairs and swap if out of order. An early-exit flag stops once a pass makes no swaps. O(n²) worst case.

rules: Early exit on a clean pass.
remember.takeaway: Bubble sort: the largest bubbles to the end each pass.
remember.formula: for i: for j<n-1-i: if a[j]>a[j+1] swap; stop if no swaps
antiSignals: Production sorting — use the library O(n log n)

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, sort it ascending using bubble sort (in place).
understanding: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; each pass 'bubbles' the largest remaining element to the end.

approaches.name: Adjacent-swap passes
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Bubble sort makes repeated passes, swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs. Each pass 'bubbles' the largest remaining element to its final position at the end.

**Why the inner bound shrinks (`n-1-i`).** After pass i, the last i elements are already the i largest, sorted and settled — so the next pass needn't touch them. Shrinking the inner bound avoids redundant comparisons.

**Why the early-exit flag matters.** If a full pass makes zero swaps, the array is already sorted and you can stop — turning the best case (already-sorted input) into O(n). Without the flag it's always O(n²).

**Stability and use.** Bubble sort is stable (equal elements keep order) and in place (O(1) space), but its O(n²) average makes it a teaching algorithm, not a production one. Know it to discuss sorting fundamentals.
hints: Each pass moves the largest unsorted element where?
Can you shrink the inner loop as elements settle?
Add a flag to stop early when a pass makes no swaps.
approaches.complexityReasoning: up to n passes of up to n comparisons → O(n²) worst/average; the swap flag makes a sorted input O(n).

java.explanation: The last i elements are already in place — skip them.
No swaps means the array is sorted; stop early.

edgeCases.behavior: Already sorted → one pass, no swaps, O(n).

pitfalls: Skipping the early-exit and always running O(n²).
Inner bound not shrinking (n-1-i), redoing settled elements.
